title: Eat the fruit (Chagigah 15b)
hookLine: Rabbi Meir found a pomegranate, ate the fruit and threw away the peel
carry: eat the fruit, drop the peel

cards: A pomegranate, split open. Red seeds packed tight, sweet and bright. Around them, a tough, bitter rind that nobody eats.
Nobody throws away the fruit because of the peel, and nobody chews the peel because they like the fruit.
The Talmud reaches for exactly this picture when it faces an uncomfortable question about Rabbi Meir and the teacher who left. Today, a fruit, a peel, and a surprising answer from heaven.

teach.h: HOW COULD MEIR LEARN FROM HIM?
teach.b: Yesterday Rabbi Meir walked behind Acher and kept learning. Tractate Chagigah doesn't let that pass quietly. It asks: how could he?
There's a teaching, built on a verse in the prophet Malachi, that you should learn Torah from a teacher only if he is like a messenger of the Lord: someone whose life matches his words.

teach.h: FOR ONE WHO KNOWS THE DIFFERENCE.
teach.b: Acher's didn't. The Talmud answers in layers. First: a beginner should be careful, but someone grown in learning can tell what to keep and what to leave.
And then a story. A sage named Rabbah bar Shila met the prophet Elijah and asked what the Holy One was doing. Elijah said: repeating teachings in the name of all the sages, except Rabbi Meir.
Why not Meir? Because he learned from Acher. And Rabbah bar Shila objected: but Rabbi Meir found a pomegranate.

teach.h: HE ATE THE FRUIT, THREW THE PEEL.
teach.b: He ate the fruit inside and threw away the peel.
And Elijah said: now God says, Meir my son says. In the story, even heaven changes how it speaks. The picture is generous, and it's demanding.
Generous, because it lets a person keep what is true and good from a teacher, a parent, a book or a place that also carried harm.

Demanding, because you have to actually tell seed from rind, and the Talmud's own caution still stands: this is for the one who knows the difference. Not every source is safe for every learner at every stage.
But the one who knows the difference isn't told to throw away the whole fruit.

how: Rabbi Meir's pomegranate is often cited in Jewish teaching when people discuss learning from mixed sources, along with the Talmud's caution that this takes maturity and discernment.

o: keep what's good from a mixed teacher, leave the rest
enjoy life's pleasures while you still can
only learn from teachers whose lives are spotless

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: the Talmud says anyone may learn from any teacher at any stage
it cautions beginners; the pomegranate is for one who knows fruit from peel.
in the story, God at first doesn't repeat Rabbi Meir's teachings
because he learned from Acher, until the pomegranate answer.
Rabbi Meir ate the whole pomegranate, peel and all
he ate the fruit inside and threw away the peel.

games.q: you're Rabbah bar Shila. Elijah tells you God won't repeat Rabbi Meir's teachings, because he learned from Acher. what do you say?
o: then Meir's teachings should be thrown out.
Meir found a pomegranate: he ate the fruit and threw away the peel.
games.why: he defends Meir with the pomegranate, and Elijah reports that God now says: Meir my son says.

practice: Bring to mind a source in your life that is mixed: a parent, a former teacher, a book you love that also has something ugly in it; if one hurt you deeply, choose a gentler one today.
Name the peel honestly, without pretending it's all fruit. Then name one seed that is still good, still sweet, still yours, and hold it.

wordCard.voice: Eat the fruit. Rabbi Meir's way with the teacher who left: keep the fruit, throw away the peel, and know which is which. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: pomegranate, the fruit in the Talmud's picture of Rabbi Meir and his teacher.

carryVoice: Your line: eat the fruit, drop the peel. Knowing which is which is the whole skill. See you tomorrow.
